title: The Vatican’s Gallery of Maps lays Italy along a 120 m corridor, split down the Apennines
body: The Gallery of Maps in the Vatican Museums is a corridor 120 m long and 6 m wide, built in 1578–1580 for Pope Gregory XIII and frescoed in under two years. Its programme was designed by [Egnazio Danti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignazio_Danti), a Dominican friar, mathematician and astronomer: 40 maps, 32 of them showing Italy’s regions in order from north to south, and eight narrower ones at the ends. Danti used the **Apennines**, Italy’s mountain spine, as the dividing line: regions on the Ligurian and Tyrrhenian seas are on the wall facing the Belvedere Courtyard, those bounded by the Alps and the Adriatic on the wall facing the Vatican Gardens. So walking the gallery is like walking up Italy along its ridge. Each regional map has a bird’s-eye view of its main city, and 51 ceiling panels tell stories of the Church set in the regions below. Danti also sat on Gregory XIII’s calendar commission; in 1574 he had found the spring equinox falling on 11 March, well before 21 March, the date the Church’s calendar assumed. The [Vatican Museums](https://www.museivaticani.va/content/museivaticani/en/collezioni/musei/galleria-carte-geografiche.html) call it the first picture of Italy, then divided into many states, as one land.

slides.prompt: In the Vatican’s Gallery of Maps, Egnazio Danti hung landlocked Umbria with the Tyrrhenian coast regions. Why?
slides.answer: Umbria lies west of the Apennines, the ridge that splits the walls
slides.detail: Danti divided Italy along its mountain spine: one wall for the regions west and south of it, the other for those bounded by the Alps and the Adriatic.

slides.alt: Animation on parchment: the Vatican's Gallery of Maps in perspective, then Italy with the Apennines as a spine. The land splits along it into a Tyrrhenian and an Adriatic half, which become the two walls of a corridor of regional maps, walked from south to north; then Danti's equinox of 1574.

slides.prompt: For each region, choose the wall of the Gallery of Maps its map hangs on, by which side of the Apennines it lies.
slides.takeaway: Danti sorted Italy by its mountain ridge, not by its coasts: landlocked Umbria joins the Tyrrhenian wall, while Piedmont, Milan and Bologna, north of the ridge, join the Adriatic one.

slides.alt: The Gallery of Maps in the Vatican Museums: a long gilded barrel vault with painted panels, and the painted maps of Italy’s regions lining both walls into the distance.

left.label: Tyrrhenian wall
left.text: Faces the Belvedere Courtyard: Liguria, Tuscany, Umbria, Lazio with Rome, Campania, Calabria, then Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica.

right.label: Adriatic wall
right.text: Faces the Vatican Gardens: Piedmont, Milan, the Venetian lands, Bologna, the Marche, Abruzzo and Apulia, down to Italy’s heel.

slides.label: painted maps in the Gallery of Maps
slides.text: 32 of Italy’s regions, in order from north to south, and 8 narrower maps at the ends: islands, four ports and two battles.

slides.question: In the Gallery of Maps, which wall holds the map of the Duchy of Milan?
options: The wall of the Adriatic side
The wall of the Tyrrhenian side
The end wall, with the ports
slides.explanation: Milan lies north of the Apennines, so its map hangs with the regions bounded by the Alps and the Adriatic, on the wall facing the Vatican Gardens.
